2.title: The Rocks That Build Themselves
2.subtitle: A reading sheet for ages 5 to 6
2.intro: Read the story. Then do each part.

blocks.prompt: How a Crystal Grows
blocks.text: Crystals grow, but they are not alive. A plant grows by making new cells. A crystal grows a different way. It is built from tiny pieces that are much too small to see. The pieces float in water. They land on the crystal and stick. Then more land on top. Layer by layer, the crystal gets bigger. You can watch it happen at home. Stir sugar into hot water until no more will dissolve. Hang a string in the jar. Wait a week. Tiny pieces of sugar leave the water and stack onto the string in neat rows. Soon the string is covered in hard, sweet crystals. People call that rock candy.

answers: no, they are not alive
tiny pieces land on it and stick, layer by layer
rock candy

3.title: The Rocks That Build Themselves
3.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 7 to 8
3.intro: Read the passage, then work through each part. You can look back at the passage any time.

blocks.prompt: Why a Crystal Has Flat Sides
blocks.text: Pick up a grain of salt and look at it through a magnifying glass. It is a cube. Not close to a cube. A real cube, with six flat faces and sharp corners. Every grain in the shaker is the same shape. That shape is not an accident. Salt is built from tiny pieces called atoms, and in salt the atoms stack in a grid, like blocks packed in a box. Each atom sits in its own spot, the same distance from its neighbors, over and over, millions of times. When a pattern that neat grows big enough to see, it shows up on the outside as flat faces. The shape of the crystal is the shape of the pattern hiding inside it. Different atoms stack in different patterns, so they build different shapes. Quartz grows six-sided columns with a point on the end. Snow grows six arms. Diamond grows a shape with eight faces. Rock hunters can often name a mineral just by looking at the shape it grew.

4.title: The Rocks That Build Themselves
4.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 9 to 10
4.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Some questions ask what you think, not just what the passage says.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Crystals grow out of dissolved mineral
Slow growth makes big crystals
Granite cooled slowly, so you can see its grains
Naica, Mexico: gypsum beams longer than a school bus
Gypsum is soft enough to scratch with a fingernail

blocks.prompt: Grown, Not Made
blocks.text: A crystal is not carved. It is grown, one layer at a time, and the way it grows decides how big it gets. Most crystals begin dissolved. Hot water deep in the ground can hold enormous amounts of dissolved mineral, the way hot tea holds more sugar than cold tea does. When that water cools, or when some of it escapes, it can no longer hold everything it was carrying. The extra mineral has to go somewhere, so it starts locking onto any solid surface it can find. Atoms settle into the pattern, more atoms settle on top of those, and the crystal thickens outward. Time is the whole story. Rush the process and you get a mess of tiny grains, because crystals start forming everywhere at once and crowd each other out. Slow it down and a few crystals grow enormous, because atoms have time to find their proper place in the pattern. That is why granite, which cooled slowly deep underground, is speckled with grains you can pick out with your eye, while lava that hardened in a day looks smooth and dull. The record for patience sits in a mine at Naica, in Mexico. Hot mineral water filled a chamber there and stayed at almost exactly the same temperature for hundreds of thousands of years. Nothing hurried it. Nothing interrupted it. The gypsum crystals that grew in that water are longer than a school bus, thicker than a person, and clear enough to see your hand through.

blocks.prompt: Answer each question in full sentences.

answers: cool water cannot hold as much dissolved mineral, so the extra locks onto a surface
atoms have time to find their proper place instead of crowding each other out
(inference: cooling speed, not the mineral, decides crystal size)
(inference: growth only continues while conditions hold steady, so a change would stop or spoil the pattern)

5.title: The Rocks That Build Themselves
5.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 11 to 12
5.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Use evidence from the text where the question asks for it.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Naica mine, Chihuahua, Mexico

Largest beams: near 40 feet, over 50 tons

blocks.prompt: The Cave of the Crystals
blocks.text: In April 2000, two brothers named Eloy and Javier Delgado were drilling a fresh tunnel about a thousand feet beneath the desert at Naica, in northern Mexico. The mine had been giving up silver, zinc, and lead for a century, and the brothers expected more of the same. What the drill broke into that day was not ore. It was a room, and the room was full of beams. They were crystals. Gypsum crystals, the same soft mineral that goes into plaster and drywall, but grown to a size nobody had ever recorded. The largest run close to forty feet long and weigh more than fifty tons. They cross the chamber at every angle, pale and translucent, like the inside of a shattered chandelier. The cave built them out of two ingredients: mineral water and time. Far below the chamber sits a body of magma that has kept the surrounding rock warm for around a million years. That heat filled the cave with water near 136 degrees Fahrenheit and then, remarkably, held it there. Just below that temperature a mineral called anhydrite comes apart in water and reassembles itself as gypsum, and it does so with almost unbelievable slowness. Slowness was the gift. Atom by atom, with no cold snap and no dry spell to interrupt the work, the crystals grew for perhaps half a million years. Visiting them nearly kills you. The chamber sits near 136 degrees Fahrenheit at close to total humidity, so water condenses inside your lungs faster than your body can shed its heat. Unprotected, a person lasts about ten minutes. Explorers went in wearing suits packed with ice, breathing chilled air through a mask, and even then they were pulled out inside an hour. The mine had kept the cave dry only by pumping groundwater away. In 2015 the pumping stopped and the water came back. The crystals are submerged again now, in the dark, resting in the warm mineral bath that made them. Almost nobody will ever see them again. They are almost certainly still growing.

6.title: The Rocks That Build Themselves
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: A crystal is one pattern repeated without error
X-ray crystallography began in 1912
Photo 51 revealed the shape of DNA in 1952
Dorothy Hodgkin mapped penicillin, B12, and insulin
Watch quartz hums 32,768 times per second
Piezoelectricity: found by the Curie brothers, 1880

blocks.prompt: The Order in Everything
blocks.text: A crystal is one of the simplest ideas in science, and one of the most useful. It is matter that has agreed on a pattern. Take a single arrangement of atoms, small enough that millions of them would fit across your fingernail. Copy it. Set the copy beside the original, exactly aligned, exactly the same distance away. Do that in every direction, a trillion times over, without one mistake. What you have built is a crystal, and the flat faces and sharp angles you can see with your eye are simply the pattern reporting itself at a scale you happen to be able to notice. The outside is an honest advertisement for the inside. That honesty turned out to be the key to the twentieth century. In 1912 a physicist named Max von Laue wondered what would happen if he fired X-rays at a crystal. Nobody could see an atom. No lens exists that can focus X-rays the way glass focuses light, and the things he wanted to look at were smaller than any light could show him. But a crystal is a repeating grid, and a repeating grid scatters waves into a pattern of bright spots. Those spots are not a picture of the atoms. They are a code, and the arrangement of the atoms can be worked backward out of it. Within a year a father and son, William and Lawrence Bragg, had turned that code into a method, and in 1915 it won them both a Nobel Prize. Lawrence was twenty-five. For the next forty years, chemistry stopped guessing. Dorothy Hodgkin used crystals to work out the structure of penicillin while the Second World War was still running, then vitamin B12, then insulin, each one a molecule nobody had ever laid eyes on. In 1952 Rosalind Franklin and her student Raymond Gosling aimed an X-ray beam at a fine thread of DNA and produced an image known as Photo 51: a blurred X of dark smudges. To an untrained eye it is nothing at all. To someone who reads diffraction it says helix, and it hands over the width, the twist, and the spacing. The shape of life was read off a photograph of scattered light. Crystals also keep your time. Squeeze a piece of quartz and it produces a small voltage, a property the Curie brothers found in 1880. Run the trick backward, feed voltage into the quartz, and it bends. Feed it a rhythm and it vibrates, and here is the part that matters: it insists on vibrating at its own frequency, fixed by the shape it was cut into and the pattern locked inside it. A watch holds a sliver of quartz cut like a tiny tuning fork, humming 32,768 times every second. A circuit halves that number fifteen times and arrives at exactly one pulse per second. The crystal is not measuring the second. The crystal is defining it. We tend to file crystals under decoration, something purple in a gift shop window. That is a strange fate for the object that let us see molecules and cut the day into pieces. A crystal is only matter that stopped improvising, and nearly everything we know about the small world we learned by asking a well behaved pattern a question and reading the answer off the light that came back.
